headline: Approved certificate allowing roof anchors and snow rails at St. John's Catholic Church, 217 York Street.
summary: The project includes 15 roof anchors, three snow rails, and replacing three crosses with mahogany. Members also approved the August 13 minutes and adopted findings for 73 Main Street and 139 Main Street, and they discussed commercial building features downtown.
decisions: Approved the August 13, 2026 meeting minutes, with all voting members in favor.
Adopted findings and decisions for 73 Main Street and 139 Main Street, with all voting members in favor.
Recorded that Commissioner Weitkamp has a conflict of interest and is recused from the discussion of 217 York Street, with all voting members in favor.
Found that replacing the three crosses at 217 York Street is ordinary maintenance that does not need Commission review, with all voting members in favor.
Approved a Certificate of Appropriateness for the roof anchor and snow rail project at 217 York Street, with all voting members in favor.

decision_evidence.quote: Commissioner Coe moved to approve the August 13th meeting minutes. Seconded by Commissioner Weitkamp. All voting members in favor, none opposed. Motion passed.
Commissioner Coe moved to adopt the findings and decisions for 73 Main Street and 139 Main Street. Seconded by Commissioner Krupke. All voting members in favor, none opposed. Motion passed.

Commissioner Coe motioned that Commissioner Weitkamp has a conflict of interest and should be recused from the discussion. Seconded by Commissioner Krupke. All voting members in favor, none opposed. Motion passed.

Commissioner Coe moved that the replacement of the three crosses is ordinary maintenance and does not need to be considered by the Commission. Seconded by Commissioner Krupke. All voting members in favor, none opposed. Motion passed.

Commissioner Coe moved that the Commission finds that, based on the findings in Parts 1-2 of Section IV of this document, the Project meets the requirements for a Certificate of Appropriateness and therefore grants a Certificate of Appropriateness for the proposed Project. Seconded by Commissioner Krupke. All voting members in favor, none opposed. Motion passed.

7:00 P.M.
 PAUL BUNYAN ROOM, CITY HALL 
73 HARLOW STREET  
MEETING MINUTES 
Commission Members Present:  Nathaniel King 
K atie Coe 
Matthew Weitkamp 
Rebecca Krupke (via Zoom) 
City Staff Present: Anja Collette, Planning Officer 
Matt Altiero, Planning Analyst 
Mike Pullen, HPC Consultant 
Ch
air King called the meeting to order at 7:00 P.M. 
______________________________________________________________________ 
Old Business:

New Business: 
3. Certificate of Appropriateness – 217 York Street – Map-Lot 055-011 – St. John’s
Catholic Church Historic Site – Applicant: Saint Paul the Apostle Parish – Owner:
Historic Preservation Commission – Meeting Minutes 
September 10th, 2026 
Roman Catholic Bishop of Portland – The applicant, Roman Catholic Bishop of 
Portland, requests approval for the installation of bronze permanent anchors and snow 
rails, the replacement of ridge flashing, and the like-for-like replacement of three crosses 
with materials suited for weather protection. The property is located at Map-Lot 055-011 
and is a historic site, St. John’s Catholic Church. Applicant: Saint Paul the Apostle 
Parish. Owner: Roman Catholic Bishop of Portland. 
 
Chair King introduced the agenda item. 
 
Commissioner Weitkamp discussed a conflict of interest, as he has a financial stake in the project.  
 
Commissioner Coe motioned that Commissioner Weitkamp has a conflict of interest and should be 
recused from the discussion. Seconded by Commissioner Krupke. All voting members in favor, none 
opposed. Motion passed. 
 
Applicant Representatives Tim Mackay and Ben Rehmeyer presented on the project. 
 
Commissioner Coe asked for more detail on the orientation of the building based off the images; the 
Applicant Representatives explained. 
 
HPC Consultant Pullen provided a summary of the work, stating the installation of 15 roof anchors, three 
snow rails at two locations, and three crosses at the gable peaks. He discussed the building’s history, 
sharing it was designed by Patrick Keeley in the Gothic Revival style and was dedicated in 1856. 
 
HPC Consultant Pullen asked if the original crosses are to be replicated – the Applicant Representatives 
responded the intent is to match the size, but the material will change to increase longevity.  
 
HPC Consultant Pullen asked how the joint between the anchors and ridge cap will be sealed – the 
Applicant Representatives discussed soldering, installing a sealant, or a combination of both strategies.  
 
The Applicant Representatives discussed that the snow guards are anchored with a slate shingle with 
bronze on the end. 
 
Chair King asked the Commission for questions. 
 
Commissioner Coe asked for details about where the installation is oriented on roof – the Applicant 
Representatives responded between buttress 3 and 4, approximately 18 feet from the buttress.  
 
Commissioner Coe asked how to proceed if the Commission evaluated all changes except for the 
installation of snow rails as ordinary maintenance – HPC Consultant Pullen discussed that the cross 
replacement is the element of the project considered ordinary maintenance.  
 
Commissioner Coe moved that the replacement of the three crosses is ordinary maintenance and does 
not need to be considered by the Commission. Seconded by Commissioner Krupke. All voting members 
in favor, none opposed. Motion passed. 
 
Chair King asked whether the rails will be visible from the street level – the Applicant Representatives 
responded they will rise approximately 4 inches above the roof. 
 
Commissioner Coe asked what the anchor caps may look like in the instance they are required to 
prevent water intrusion – the Applicant Representatives responded they would appear as a sleeve or

flashing cap. Commissioner Coe noted she does not think the caps would increase the profile more, and 
the project makes sense to improve safety. 
 
The Applicant Representatives asked about installing a bird deterrent on top of the crosses. Planning 
Officer Collette asked if there is an issue with having birds on them. Chair King expressed that so long 
as the deterrent isn’t visible, it is unlikely to be an issue. Krupke expressed concern about what the bird 
deterrent spikes would look like.   
 
Commissioner Krupke asked about the original material of the crosses. The Applicant Representatives 
said they believe the original material was spruce or hemlock, and they are proposing mahogany.  
 
Chair King opened public comment – there were none. Public comment closed. 
 
Commissioner Coe moved that the Commission finds that the procedural background was met for the 
requirements of the project. Seconded by Commissioner Krupke. All voting members in favor, none 
opposed. Motion passed. 
 
Commissioner Coe moved that the Commission finds that, based on Exhibits 1-2, the application 
satisfied Historic Preservation Code §148-9A requiring that any alteration of the historic structure will 
preserve or enhance its historical and architectural character. Seconded by Commissioner Krupke. All 
voting members in favor, none opposed. Motion passed. 
 
Commissioner Coe moved that the Commission finds that Part 2, Sections 1, 5, 6, 7, and 8, and Part 3, 
Sections 1, 2, and 3, as not applicable to the project. Seconded by Commissioner Krupke. All voting 
members in favor, none opposed. Motion passed. 
 
Commissioner Coe moved that the Commission finds that, based on Exhibits 1-2, the application 
satisfies Historic Preservation Code § 148-9B(2)(b) requiring that rehabilitation work does not destroy 
the distinguishing qualities nor character of the structure and its environment. Seconded by 
Commissioner Krupke. All voting members in favor, none opposed. Motion passed. 
 
Commissioner Coe moved that the Commission finds that, based on Exhibits 1-2, the application 
satisfies Historic Preservation Code §148-9B(2)(c) requiring that, while repair is preferable to 
replacement, in the event that replacement of deteriorated architectural features is necessary, the 
feature being replaced in color, design, texture and other visual qualities and, where economically and 
technically feasible, materials. Seconded by Commissioner Krupke. All voting members in favor, none 
opposed. Motion passed. 
 
Commissioner Coe moved that the Commission finds that, based on Exhibits 1-2, the application 
satisfies Historic Preservation Code § 148-9B(2)(d) requiring that distinctive stylistic features or 
examples of skilled craftsmanship which characterize historic structures is not damaged or destroyed, 
wherever possible. Seconded by Commissioner Krupke. All voting members in favor, none opposed. 
Motion passed. 
 
Commissioner Coe moved that the Commission finds that, based on Exhibits 1-2, the application 
satisfies Historic Preservation Code § 148-9B(2)(i) requiring that, wherever possible, all alterations to 
structures shall be done in such a manner that if they were to be removed in the future the essential 
form and integrity of the original structure would be unimpaired. Seconded by Commissioner Krupke. All 
voting members in favor, none opposed. Motion passed. 
 
Commissioner Coe moved that the Commission finds that, based on the findings in Parts 1-2 of Section 
IV of this document, the Project meets the requirements for a Certificate of Appropriateness and

Krupke. All voting members in favor, none opposed. Motion passed. 
 
4. Discuss Commercial Character-Defining Features in the Historic Districts 
 
HPC Consultant Pullen presented on character-defining features of commercial buildings in Bangor.  
 
HPC Consultant Pullen shared the history of the Bangor House, a building designed by Isaiah Rogers 
and built in 1833, with additions attributed to Charles Bryant.  
 
HPC Consultant Pullen reminded the Commission of § 148-9B(2)(b), stating “rehabilitation work shall 
not destroy the distinguishing qualities nor character of the structure and its environment.” He also 
discussed the Secretary of Interior’s Standards of Rehabilitation and Guidelines for Rehabilitation, which 
defines a character-defining feature as “a prominent or distinctive aspect, quality, or characteristic of a 
historic property that contributes significantly to its physical character. Structures, objects, vegetation, 
spatial relationships, views, furnishings, decorative details, and materials may be such features.” He 
recommended the Commission to reference Cultural & Architectural Resource Management Archive 
(CARMA) forms to receive additional information about properties’ features. Planning Officer Collette 
discussed that staff have added CARMA forms to the City’s Parcel Viewer. 
 
HPC Consultant Pullen discussed common elements on downtown Bangor storefronts, such as 
cornices, bulkheads, sign bands, and recessed entrances. He discussed the popularity of cast iron use 
in buildings downtown, and that storefronts were largely composed of large windows.  
 
HPC Consultant Pullen discussed that around 1905, metal clamped storefront systems became 
popularized, with some downtown buildings having a fine perimeter of metal to set windows in. 
Commissioner Coe asked if this trend was occurring regionally or nationally – Pullen responded 
nationally. Pullen shared that transoms were a popular feature to help with lighting within a store. 
 
HPC Consultant Pullen discussed the common commercial building architectural styles in Bangor, 
including: 
• Federal 
• Greek Revival 
• Queen Anne 
• Second Empire 
• Romanesque 
• Italianate 
• Second Empire 
• Neo-Classical  
• Prairie Style 
• Deco/Moderne 
• Modern 
 
Commissioner Krupke asked what the prairie-style building in Bangor contains – HPC Consultant Pullen 
anticipates it houses electrical equipment. Krupke complimented the maintenance of the building. 
 
HPC Consultant Pullen discussed the benefit of the pre-application meetings.
